title: The High Priestess: Noticing What Has Not Been Said

quickTake.upright: Be still and observe. Some information has not surfaced yet.
quickTake.reversed: Feelings may be tangled with guesses, or something has remained unsaid.

hook: The High Priestess holds a scroll without fully unrolling it. She draws attention to an easily overlooked fact: information can be right before your eyes and still be incomplete.

sections.title: The Scroll Lets Us Read Only Part of It
sections.bodyMarkdown:
She sits upright between two tall pillars. On the left of the picture stands a black pillar bearing a white B; on the right, a white pillar bearing a black J. Blue-and-white robes fall to the ground, a white cross rests on her chest, and her crown consists of curved hornlike forms on either side of a central disk. A yellow crescent moon rests against the lower part of her robe.

A scroll marked TORA lies diagonally before her lap, partly concealed by fabric. Behind her, a veil is patterned with pomegranates and palms; narrow gaps at its sides reveal a blue background. Figure, pillars, and veil form a stable frontal composition: we are allowed to see some things and kept outside others. She neither beckons to us nor displays the scroll's entire contents.

[View the RWS artwork checked for this article](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RWS_Tarot_02_High_Priestess.jpg)

When looking at the scroll, practice not filling in what is concealed. You know it exists and that only part is visible, but you do not know the remaining words. This distinguishes “the information is incomplete” from “I already know the truth.” The contrast between the pillars also leaves room for different interpretations; it cannot simply divide things into good and bad camps. A little blue is genuinely visible behind the veil, but this does not license us to invent events behind it. Bring that restraint into daily life: first record a feeling, then wait for a question, observation, or new material before deciding whether it has support.

sections.title: Esoteric Knowledge Is Not Proof of Someone's Secret
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Waite explicitly explains the partly concealed scroll as meaning that some things are spoken and others implied. He connects the veil and pillars with hidden religious knowledge and interprets the High Priestess within his own occult system. “Hidden” here has a historical context; it is not an accusation that someone in real life is keeping a secret.

This article uses the picture to practice patient observation: allow yourself not to know for now, while noticing feelings that have not yet formed into complete language. Intuition may indicate where another question would be useful, but it still needs to be checked against real-world evidence.

[Read Waite's original English text for this card](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar02.htm)

sections.title: Understanding the Upright Card
sections.bodyMarkdown:
Upright often suits a moment for listening, observing, or waiting for information to become ready. Let someone finish speaking before replying. Notice unstated assumptions in material you read. When making a choice, identify why a particular detail gives you pause.

Quiet does not mean doing nothing. You can take notes, ask questions, keep judgments provisional, and put limits around waiting. Her scroll reminds us that knowing what you have not read is itself an important form of understanding.

sections.title: Understanding the Reversed Card
sections.bodyMarkdown:
This article focuses reversal on two possible distortions: treating a strong feeling as an immediate conclusion, or suppressing feelings and questions until others cannot understand your silence. Both call for making something vague clearer.

Write separate lists headed “Facts I have observed,” “My feelings,” and “Causes I am guessing.” If the three blur together, hold off on conclusions. If the facts are already sufficient and you still keep waiting, consider whether it is time to state a need or respond.

sections.title: Distinguishing Related Meanings
sections.bodyMarkdown: Both the High Priestess and the Moon encounter the unknown. The High Priestess more readily focuses attention on what is not yet disclosed or articulated, and on patient listening. The Moon places more emphasis on how imagination pulls at us under incomplete information. The High Priestess also differs from the Hermit: the Hermit may actively pursue a question, while she first acknowledges that the whole content cannot yet be read. If a clear answer already exists in real life, do not repeatedly overturn the person's words by invoking “hidden meanings.” Suspending judgment needs a reason and a time limit. Long waiting without new information can sometimes merely postpone a question you could already ask.

sections.title: Reading Oral Histories: Leave the Question Open
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Xiaoning asks, “How should I handle contradictions in this community oral-history account?”

Known facts: Two interviewees remember different years for an event. An old photograph is labeled only with the season. The editor wants the piece finalized quickly, and Xiaoning feels that one passage sounds like something that happened in another year. She draws the upright High Priestess in the research-method position.

The partly concealed scroll corresponds to having material in hand while important context remains unread. Her feeling is worth using as a direction for research, but cannot directly override the interviewees' memories. Here, the upright High Priestess encourages retaining the discrepancy and listening carefully, rather than treating the most compelling version as the truth. The different memories may also concern two similar events.

Another possibility: If a verifiable event notice later turns up, the date will have a more reliable basis. If it remains impossible to establish, the piece should explain that recollections differ. Drawing this card is no reason to assume the archive must conceal a dramatic reversal.

A practical next step: In follow-up interviews, clarify the location, people present, and events before and after, without leading anyone toward a particular year. Leave the points requiring verification in the draft, agree on a checking deadline, then decide whether to state a definite date or retain wording that acknowledges uncertainty.

sections.title: Say What Feels Uncomfortable Rather Than Waiting to Be Understood
sections.bodyMarkdown:
**Original fictional case.** Ruoxi asks, “Why do I always feel a little uneasy after friends gather at my home?”

Known facts: She welcomes friends dropping by but dislikes unplanned overnight stays. The last two times she said, “It's fine,” then spent a long time cleaning alone afterwards. Her friends do not yet know this matters to her. She draws the reversed High Priestess in the communication-obstacle position.

This example fits “feelings left unspoken” more than “intuition reveals someone's ulterior motive.” The concealed scroll suggests a boundary that has not been communicated: Ruoxi already knows what she needs but expects others to read it in her silence. Reversal shifts attention from analyzing her friends' motives to arrangements she can express clearly. Her discomfort is a real feeling; she does not have to prove her friends wrong before it deserves discussion.

Another possibility: If she has clearly said that overnight stays are not an option and others keep crossing that boundary, the issue becomes their behavior and disregard of a stated limit. Advising her simply to “say something” would then overlook communication that has already happened. The sequence of events must be checked again.

A practical next step: Before the next invitation, specify the finishing time and that there will be no overnight stays, allowing friends to choose another venue. After the conversation, record their actual response. Use new experiences together to judge whether the relationship can adjust, rather than replacing one direct, calm conversation with guesses.

sections.title: A Small Exercise
sections.bodyMarkdown: Choose one unresolved question and write three facts, three feelings, and three guesses about it. Circle one question that can be checked. Verify only that today, without rushing to fill every blank.

sections.title: A Common Misreading
sections.bodyMarkdown: The High Priestess does not mean “your intuition is always right,” nor is she a reason to wait indefinitely. The black and white of the pillars are first of all a contrast within the picture; they cannot directly assign good and evil to two real people.

# The High Priestess: Noticing What Has Not Been Said

Upright in a sentence: Be still and observe. Some information has not surfaced yet.

Reversed in a sentence: Feelings may be tangled with guesses, or something has remained unsaid.

The High Priestess holds a scroll without fully unrolling it. She draws attention to an easily overlooked fact: information can be right before your eyes and still be incomplete.

## The Scroll Lets Us Read Only Part of It

She sits upright between two tall pillars. On the left of the picture stands a black pillar bearing a white B; on the right, a white pillar bearing a black J. Blue-and-white robes fall to the ground, a white cross rests on her chest, and her crown consists of curved hornlike forms on either side of a central disk. This distinguishes “the information is incomplete” from “I already know the truth.” The contrast between the pillars also leaves room for different interpretations; it cannot simply divide things into good and bad camps. A little blue is genuinely visible behind the veil, but this does not license us to invent events behind it. Bring that restraint into daily life: first record a feeling, then wait for a question, observation, or new material before deciding whether it has support.

## Esoteric Knowledge Is Not Proof of Someone's Secret

Waite explicitly explains the partly concealed scroll as meaning that some things are spoken and others implied. He connects the veil and pillars with hidden religious knowledge and interprets the High Priestess within his own occult system. “Hidden” here has a historical context; it is not an accusation that someone in real life is keeping a secret.

This article uses the picture to practice patient observation: allow yourself not to know for now, while noticing feelings that have not yet formed into complete language. Intuition may indicate where another question would be useful, but it still needs to be checked against real-world evidence.

[Read Waite's original English text for this card](https://original.sacred-texts.com/tarot/pkt/pktar02.htm)

## Understanding the Upright Card

Upright often suits a moment for listening, observing, or waiting for information to become ready. Let someone finish speaking before replying. Notice unstated assumptions in material you read. When making a choice, identify why a particular detail gives you pause.

Quiet does not mean doing nothing. You can take notes, ask questions, keep judgments provisional, and put limits around waiting. Her scroll reminds us that knowing what you have not read is itself an important form of understanding.

## Understanding the Reversed Card

This article focuses reversal on two possible distortions: treating a strong feeling as an immediate conclusion, or suppressing feelings and questions until others cannot understand your silence. Both call for making something vague clearer.

Write separate lists headed “Facts I have observed,” “My feelings,” and “Causes I am guessing.” If the three blur together, hold off on conclusions. If the facts are already sufficient and you still keep waiting, consider whether it is time to state a need or respond.

## Distinguishing Related Meanings

Both the High Priestess and the Moon encounter the unknown. The High Priestess more readily focuses attention on what is not yet disclosed or articulated, and on patient listening. The Moon places more emphasis on how imagination pulls at us under incomplete information. The High Priestess also differs from the Hermit: the Hermit may actively pursue a question, while she first acknowledges that the whole content cannot yet be read. If a clear answer already exists in real life, do not repeatedly overturn the person's words by invoking “hidden meanings.” Suspending judgment needs a reason and a time limit. Long waiting without new information can sometimes merely postpone a question you could already ask.

## Reading Oral Histories: Leave the Question Open

**Original fictional case.** Xiaoning asks, “How should I handle contradictions in this community oral-history account?”

Known facts: Two interviewees remember different years for an event. An old photograph is labeled only with the season. The editor wants the piece finalized quickly, and Xiaoning feels that one passage sounds like something that happened in another year. She draws the upright High Priestess in the research-method position.

Her feeling is worth using as a direction for research, but cannot directly override the interviewees' memories. Here, the upright High Priestess encourages retaining the discrepancy and listening carefully, rather than treating the most compelling version as the truth. The different memories may also concern two similar events.

Leave the points requiring verification in the draft, agree on a checking deadline, then decide whether to state a definite date or retain wording that acknowledges uncertainty.

## Say What Feels Uncomfortable Rather Than Waiting to Be Understood

**Original fictional case.** Ruoxi asks, “Why do I always feel a little uneasy after friends gather at my home?”

Known facts: She welcomes friends dropping by but dislikes unplanned overnight stays. The last two times she said, “It's fine,” then spent a long time cleaning alone afterwards. Her friends do not yet know this matters to her. She draws the reversed High Priestess in the communication-obstacle position.

This example fits “feelings left unspoken” more than “intuition reveals someone's ulterior motive.” The concealed scroll suggests a boundary that has not been communicated: Ruoxi already knows what she needs but expects others to read it in her silence. ## A Small Exercise

Choose one unresolved question and write three facts, three feelings, and three guesses about it. Circle one question that can be checked. Verify only that today, without rushing to fill every blank.

## A Common Misreading

The High Priestess does not mean “your intuition is always right,” nor is she a reason to wait indefinitely. The black and white of the pillars are first of all a contrast within the picture; they cannot directly assign good and evil to two real people.
